Cool game. It's got different elements to the game play so you're not doing the same thing over and over. You can also choose different strategies by the upgrades and cards you select along the adventure. This game has lot's of replayability.

It's easy to mistake Demon's Mirror for just another Slay the Spire clone. It's not afraid to wear it's inspiration on its sleeve, for sure, but the interaction between cards and the match-3 board make for something special and unique. You can get really strategic in setting up combos, and you need to because each encounter is tough. I was a big fan of the original Puzzle Quest, using spells and abilities to manipulate the board, and this has some of that feel. Definitely not for everyone, but once you wrap your head around the mechanics, Demon's Mirror is super satisfying.

The deckbuilder genre is heavily saturated and afraid to innovate from its core formula. This game is fun, but I don't think the tile-matching is enough to overcome what is essentially the exact same problem-solving set in StS. The tile matching is a fun gimmick but the game focuses too much on the admittedly boring cards at the beginning of each run (pay 1 mana gain 4 shield, pay 1 mana deal 4 dmg etc.) and not enough on the games core feature of tile-matching. And I don't think a game where every run all I'm doing is paying 2 mana for 12 shield until I get some cool combos is something I want to ante up for the umpteenth time.

[h3] Short and Lazy Review [/h3] Fuse Slay the Spire with a chain-3 game, and you have Demon’s Mirror. Key note. Chain-3, not Match-3. With Match-3, you swap the position of board symbols to create a 3, 4 or 5 block. With Chain-3, you drag a line through as many symbols of the same kind as you can, so long as they are adjacent, orthogonally or diagonally. [h3] Concise Review [/h3] Set aside the chain-3 board temporarily, and Demon’s Mirror follows the Slay-a-like formula closely. # Begin with a starter deck and a starter artefact / trinket unique to a character, which strongly influences what they are better at # Choose your path on a branching map of nodes with battles, Elite battles, rest sites, shops, events and deck manipulation sites # Progress through multiple acts, each act ending in a boss fight # Battles are a turn-based card-playing tightrope of trying to deal damage whilst avoiding taking damage, and wins result in card and coin rewards # During a run, you add, remove and upgrade cards, gain permanent passively run-changing trinkets and single-use scrolls Then what it does differently, which also changes all the card-based play, is give you a 6x6 board of gems, representing attack, defence, a form of power-up and a form of limit-break currency, 4 total. You have the 3 energy points, same as Slay, initially, but you split them between playing cards or creating chains. Each battle turn then presents a tactical dilemma, what is the best combination of cards and chains? [h3] Highlights? [/h3] [u] Super slick and responsive [/u] Slay has a magical quality of a near frictionless sequence of card-select, drag to target, release, outcome, with immediate feedback and that little dopamine hit that accompanies it. Demon’s Mirror has that, 100%. Everything executes slickly and feels goldilocks, just right. [u] Simple innovation > great tactical challenge [/u] Many turns give you a wonderful little tactical dilemma. On any given turn, you may have choices like these: # Play 2-3 chains but no cards # Play 3 or more cards, but no chains # Split your energy between chains and cards Which is the best will also change based on how you can change the board state *before* chaining, through cards – often 0 cost – that destroy, convert or move gems around. You have a LOT of scope for setting up over several turns for a huge attack, for example, by removing other types of gems from the board to create a long chain of attack gems, applying a vulnerable debuff to enemies, and a chain buff to yourself. [u] Great synergy between cards and board [/u] Many cards can manipulate the board state, and it appears – initially – viable to really lean in to either a card-heavy or a board-heavy deck. The cards and the board interact with each other – a lot – requiring careful thought both in battle and in the overall deck building. [h3] Caveats? [/h3] [u] Learning Curve [/u] Take the learning curve of any deckbuilder – it can be tough initially as you try and figure out what the heck makes a viable deck. This has that challenge AND then the added complexity of the chain-3 side. This is not necessarily a bad thing, but I could imagine that non-veterans of both genres might find the learning pretty harsh initially. [h3] Meta Progression [/h3] Writing this only 3-4 run attempts in, I can say little just yet. There *are* things to unlock, including the core characters and buffs and debuffs that can be applied to an entire run to change the challenge level.

It's... alright. It combines two of my favorite genres into a competent, delightful package, but it just lacks that [i]oomph[/i] factor that beckons "just one more round!" The biggest issue I have is the [i]slog[/i]; fights can take [i]forever[/i], with some enemies buffing every round or making copies of themselves while you wait for [b]two[/b] RNGs to line up: both your card draw and the board draw. It's like a see-saw where you have the perfect board but none of the cards, or all your OP cards but a board of weak chains. Eventually you have to start spending your resources instead of wasting turns and taking damage, and most rounds end up with you nickel-and-diming your way through battles instead of those rare occasions where it all lines up. The best feeling about match-3 games is getting killer chains, but they usually only amount to single-turn advantages in this game. There's very little in the way of snowballing OP combos, and they usually take several turns just to set up because you're too busy dinking and diving just to stay afloat. There's some cool concepts and synergies to be found, but the three characters feel like one or two-trick ponies, making replay value scarce. It feels a little barren content-wise, and I'd be surprised to see anyone but masochists with more than 20 hours. The game cribs from existing genres and combines them into something unique, but it's just not enough to sustain long-term interest. It's definitely worth a shot if you're into this mash-up, but I'd wait until there's a sale. I just found myself wanting to play other games instead of thirsting to jump right back in.

[h1]三消+爬塔，门槛偏高，好玩但不耐玩[/h1] 核心玩法是把三消作为额外的元素加到卡牌战斗的框架里，相当于多了一层复杂度。由于每回合既要计算卡牌数值，又要规划方块堆的位置，高难度下对于策略和计算的要求甚至比很多经典DBG还要高，玩起来很有挑战性，游戏的门槛相较于市面上大部分DBG来说是偏高的。 卡组构筑方面基本的逻辑和爬塔类似，有提数值上限的能力牌，有攻防牌，有过牌卡。最核心的差异就是来自和三消机制联动的面板控制卡和方块伤害卡。比较好的地方在于巨石节点每次删2牌，商店可以花钱敲牌，所以基础卡组最后是能勉强删掉大半的，牌组的可构筑性还是比较高，很少出现某些烂DBG那种纯看发牌员脸色吃饭的局。但这个游戏主打不是运转流，基本上很难有无限牌组，主要还是玩数值。不要以爬塔运转流的思路来抓牌，不然会死很惨，真要按爬塔思路来，也得是按爬塔nosl大牌组打数值的思路来抓。因为基础牌的数值太低，前期无论遇到什么垃圾过渡卡都得抓，不然输出防御端都会吃紧，抓着抓着就成大牌组垃圾堆了。 三消机制和战斗的联动还是比较有新意的，有传统攻防，有用来提升数值的精粹，有相当于攒大招用的水晶，以及各种怪塞的负面方块。由于这个游戏会塞负面方块的怪特别特别多，导致牌组里一般必备用来专门处理负面方块牌的方块伤害卡，不然某些怪就是纯坐牢了。 三个角色的设计也算是各有特点。但这里点名批评一下狼人，狼人的机制基本上是最无趣的，理论上就是每回合给2费白嫖一次链接，数值提升基本体现在力量端，伤害提升很看精粹。作为默认角色来说和传统DBG区分度最低，但实际强度又不如传统DBG典型力量角色，导致作为新玩家上手第一感觉会是觉得这个三消机制偏鸡肋，其实不是，就是狼人有点菜。龙人是防御端强于输出端的慢热角色，靠精粹->支配输出，配合能力给支配或者支配翻倍卡，不过由于洞察是可跨回合累计，每回合的费用灵活性远比狼哥强（狼人跨回合就没了），加上有敏捷加防御数值，后期生存力远超过狼人，算是有点像传统DBG里的敏捷模板。蛙人感觉是策略性最高也最好玩的角色，导体方块给的减费非常灵活，输出端数值主要靠专注和电击两个路线，防御端也有加固这种类似鸡煲遗传算法的神卡（这玩意比遗传强太多了）。 其他优点的话，美术、音乐、UI都算中规中矩吧，不算特别亮眼，但也不会很出戏，整体完成度非常高，对于小公司做的独游来说，这个完成度非常厉害了。 然后说一下，缺点：不耐玩。为什么不耐玩，这个原因就很复杂了。 首先卡牌和怪物的数值肯定还需要多打磨一下，很多一层小怪见面打你15+，然后你3费起手，1费防御只防4，那不就只能掉大血吗。而且很多怪会塞20+伤害的敌方方块，导致很多时候拿卡也好路线也好，都只能选择最稳妥的策略，有些牌你看着感觉能搭配出不错的效果，但实际上根本没法拿，很容易鬼抽。鬼抽的最大原因在于你每回合要做的事情比纯DBG要更多，既要打攻防牌、能力牌，又要调整方块位置，又要连方块，要干的事情太多了，抽牌还是和纯DBG一样每回合摸5，那这就注定鬼抽概率增大，高难度下只能靠卖血打。我建议是每回合抽6会好很多，不要看别的DBG是抽5你也就抽5，你这抽5让面板机制就很难用。 其次，战斗带来的正反馈比较低，或者更简单说，爽感不足。难度是很高了，但是完成高链接带来的收益其实没有那么大。比如我规划半天去凑一个10+的伤害链，可能不如直接打个5+精粹链然后打个打击，或者甚至直接打双打击得了。那这个高链接的收益效果就很低，事实上我只有打蛙人的时候因为导体方块才会去凑高链接，狼人龙人的超高链接很难凑，也不值得专门去凑。而且这个游戏没有什么真正意义上能靠单饰品（遗物）改变游戏玩法的，所以运气成分其实是偏低的，这一点对于肉鸽来说，其实不是什么好事，因为很多肉鸽玩家是需要时不时有一局天胡来爽一爽的。这个遇到天胡局的概率不能太高，否则就太容易了，但概率也不能太低，甚至几乎没有，那肉鸽玩家爽不到也不好玩。包括打boss的时候，我是没有感觉到我是用【牌组】取胜的，大部分局我只感觉我是慢慢磨死的boss。与之相反的，就是负反馈很强，或者说给玩家的挫败感又很足。很典型就是怪塞的负面方块太多了，而且防御端的不足导致容易掉大血，进一步让玩家感到挫败。还有一个很典型的就是boss饰品，几乎所有的负面效果都太过于恶心人了（你想象一下假如爬塔里boss遗物都是金冠绿帽这种级别）。提升感觉上应该让链接根据长度有一个梯度递增会好一点，比如5+以上每个变成+1.5，10+以上每个+2，来鼓励玩家去规划长链接。饰品、卡牌需要有一些能真正单卡单饰品就能对游戏局内产生质变的，目前这个游戏没有这种东西。 以目前游戏的状态，我感觉是大概20+小时打完三个角色最高难度应该就不会有动力再开一把了。因为游戏目前就只有新意，有挑战性，就是重复游玩价值真的不高。我可以看的到大概打10把都是类似的局，没什么带来质变的卡牌和饰品，牌组组起来大同小异。当然，游戏是好游戏，作为小体量独游DBG来说值得一玩，也不是所有的游戏都要做成重复游玩价值的那种类型。但如果开发组想要让游戏更耐玩的话，那要走的路还有很远。

Solid card battler rougelike with chain-3 mechanic. The Slay the Spire inspiration is obvious, but the inclusion of the chain-3 grid really adds to the decision making and puzzling out each turn. The game can be quite challenging, and some cards and enemies could probably do with a few small tweaks, but the vast majority of the content and core gameplay is very solid and exceptionally polished. I also want to say that the music has been excellent and card art is fantastic, especially ones with expressions on them; I've laughed at quite a few of them! If you're a fan of Slay the Spire or similar deckbuilders and the chain-3 mechanic intrigues you, this is a solid recommend.

[h1]First Impression[/h1] I've done several runs now. 2 with all the characters at least, Where the dragon seemed like the character I synergized the most with, being that you get free cards to play when you chain anything, as long as you keep your card requirement low. (Already incentive not to use higher energy cards, VERY BAD, DOESN'T Incentivize experimentation.) The furthest I've gotten is the third world. and I was royally screwed in my first encounter because there were two enemies that wanted to attack for an upwards of about 40 damage and that's literally impossible to block unless you have insane luck. I started getting to the point where if I had low HP and kept getting bad RNG on the board and cards, I'd just slog and end it early so I could start another run where I didn't make the mistake of picking up cool, but very niche cards that I'd never find a use for. The run where I made it to world 3 was one of my worse runs. but RNG kept giving me godlike chains and cards exactly when I needed them. it felt great until the run was over and I realized that this game isn't very skill based. you just get lucky, or you barely scrape by while trying to fight back against your terrible odds, and inevitably die to some BS in one battle because you stalled for too long. I see a lot of people comparing this to Slay the Spire... I wonder how true that really is because I never played it. [h2]Pros[/h2] >The mix of both worlds, Deck builder, and Chain 3 is very VERY well done. it feels good to get a big chain in the first world that just smashes enemies. >There are events that help you out on your journey, and there's a lot of variety. with shops, Treasure chests, upgrades for cards, removing cards, all to help customize the run on the fly. >Every enemy does it's own special thing to the Chain 3 board, there's a lot of different outcomes. >Each character has a unique playstyle that changes the way you play the game. [h2]Cons[/h2] >Characters are objectively worse than others. even though I played the Dragon the most it's probably the worst charatcer in the game. >If you have any cards that require 3 energy you won't use them period, by the time you can, you've already won the battle, and don't need it anymore because the threats are all dead. >Better cards require more energy and more often than not YOU DON'T GET MORE ENERGY TO COUNTER BALANCE THIS. >Most cards are too niche and require such a specific scenario that you're throwing your game if you grab them. >Some cards are so good that if you don't grab them you're throwing. >The game is boring when you're trying to min max and play effectively instead of for fun. (Burn bad cards, force less RNG.) >If you stall out a battle and try to be tactical, you get punished by buff stacking enemies. all enemies often have a means to infinity scale damage and YOU don't. >Some Elites tend to spam tiles onto your board and it makes getting big combos impossible. Setting up becomes tedious instead of tactical. >Trinkets do so little, honestly felt like half of them did nothing at all. And by the time you get one that would have synergized with something, you don't have the means to make it work. >Battling gives you so little in return, you'll get further avoiding all but the first 2 battles in your run with the same odds of winning or losing. >Some, if not most combat mechanics feel like BS. the lack of power scaling for your own character (like permanent upgrades for this run only.) don't exist. you're stuck with the hand that was dealt to you, no pun intended. >You have to get really lucky to have a good run. and you have to beat impossible odds to win. >The game isn't hard, it's unfair. Hades is hard, but fair. Spirit Fall is hard, but fair. Backpack Hero isn't Hard, but it's Fair all the same and can be made harder with challenges. >The game has a Challenge window, but good luck getting to the point where you unlock any of them. >I'm probably not even listing all the flaws for this game. [h2]Neutral[/h2] The game has a Challenge window, among those is things that can make the game easier. but like I said before, it's all down to RNG so... I enabled all of them and died to my first Elite enemy. when I've killed 3 Elites in a row without those settings before. [h2]Conclusion[/h2] Might play a few more runs but honestly this game needs changes NOW. Want a fair game that won't make you feel like you're bad and it's your fault your bad? don't play this game. Want a game that's skillful and implementing strategy can get you a flawless? don't play this game. Masochist? play this game :)

Interesting mix of deckbuilder and match-3. Surprisingly deep, after 50 hours I still find myself thinking "wait, I could have done better by doing this..." The game is rather on the difficult side, but not too punishing so far even at Ascension 7. The game could benefit from additional content, in its current version I keep running into the same enemies, bosses, events. There are also not a lot of boss relics to choose from, etc. but it's still enjoyable.

I already had a lot of fun with the demo and the full game doesn't disappoint. This is not just another slay the spire clone. It combines known elements from Puzzle Quest/Ironcast and Slay the Spire into something special. And most importantly - something fun! Your have to juggle between traditional card play and match 3 puzzles and many cards can manipulate the puzzle grid in interesting ways. It definitely deserves more attention than what it is currently getting.

打通了Demo觉得一般，本来是不想买正式版的。但无奈我是多年资深卡牌玩家 + 多年资资深骨灰级三消玩家，对于这种玩法实在是抵抗不住，买了正式版，发现正式版中一开始给了另外一个角色，是Demo中没有的角色，这个角色的三消玩法爽度远远高于Demo中给的那个角色。 你小子可以啊，Demo留了一手是吧。 ———— 3小时感想： 商店里可以花钱多次升级牌。 牌的设计真和当年玩杀戮尖塔时候一样令人耳目一新，同时又与杀戮尖塔机制差不太远，上手迅速。甚至很多地方的细节设计水平，高于杀戮尖塔。

Most other games have done this genre better. The chain 3 mechanics are...interesting, but ultimately, they slow the run down, and they're not all that captivating. Kudos for trying to break free from the conventional, but it's not for me.

[h1][b] TLDR: Decent CCG with a unique matching board concept. Largely fails to impress due to majority of cards being subpar for deck mechanics. [/b] [/h1] [h1]PROS: [/h1] ✅Interesting gameplay mechanics with the matching board ✅Solid deck themes ✅Good “Customizable” difficulty [h1]CONS: [/h1] ➖The matching board attacks can be too punishing at times ➖Uncreative from a roguelike card perspective (Almost a copy of Slay the Spire) ➖Double the RNG with match board and decks ➖Many cards and trinkets are just plain bad You’re going to see me mention Slay the Spire a ton here, so here is my review for comparison's sake: https://steamcommunity.com/id/Synikx/recommended/646570?snr=1_5_9__402 [h1] [b] Content (Game world/Narrative/Length) – [3/10] [/b] [/h1] Game World: Demon’s Mirror (DM) takes place in a game world that is very similar to Slay the Spire (StS) - you have your battle world and the pathing map. The pathing map is nearly identical to StS, you have your battles/elites, bonfires, shops, and events. Just some mechanics are flipped around, like shops don’t offer discard options, they only do upgrades. The battle world is where DM really changes things up, mostly through the matching board that inhabits the entire right side of the screen. Other than the matching board, you have your enemies, trinkets, scrolls (potions) and can easily view all their information and enemy intents. The matching board is interesting how integrated it is into the gameplay, but I’ll cover that more in the mechanics area. Overall, aside from the matching board, DM has an almost 1:1 match to StS. While imitation is the best form of flattery, and StS is one of my favorite games, I can’t help but acknowledge how absurdly similar they are. It's like the devs played StS and decided to remake the entire game with very slight changes, at least from the game world perspective. Mechanically things start to diverge, but it's almost shocking how much of an obvious influence StS was on DM. Narrative: Small and insignificant story. There is some semblance of a story and how the end is connected to the beginning, but it's not the point of the game. Length: It can be relatively short, like all roguelikes, you can complete a single run within an hour or two. Single runs are generally slower here in DM than StS. The true value in the length is the replayability, and I think that DM has less reasons to play it repeatedly. [h1][b] Gameplay (Mechanics/Difficulty) – [6/10] [/b] [/h1] Mechanics: This is where the tiny nuances of DM start to differ from StS, thankfully. So, right off the bat the biggest part of DM that differentiates itself is the matching board. You can match like icons infinitely touching and diagonally. You have 4 match options - shield, attack, and 2 different resources green and purple. Green powers up card abilities, but fades slowly over each turn. Purple allows you to do 1 of 3 options, unique to each character. Speaking of characters, there are 3 options - your more attack-focused brawler, the damage-over-time type, and the combo-focused DoT type. I’m very much oversimplifying here, but I do feel like each character is different enough to where it's not so much an obvious copy of StS as the game world is. The matching board integrates nicely mechanically with each character - each has different methods of utilizing the board to compliment their kit. I think for me the problem comes with the cards itself. Most of the cards I’ve seen, especially “Build-defining” rare cards like you get after boss fights, are just boring at best and detrimental at worst. I would often struggle to find any good cards to add to my deck. I completed 1 winning run as Wulf and ended it with about ~15 cards in my deck, skipping tons, to create a strength deck that used a multi-attack card to one-shot enemies. It just feels like poor design when a huge amount of your cards do not feel exciting to get in a CCG game. So is DM better than StS? I don’t think so, but I also don’t think it's bad. I applaud the match board, but I do wish there were cards that focused on using it 100% instead of just being a side component. It seems like each character has a sort of build to focus on, but each build only uses the board to collect green resources, while the others are more of an option if you need them. This leads to the board being underutilized because you have attack and defense in your deck, while the purple buffs are ehh… TBH, I think the board should be buffed to make it more useful - 2x attack and 2x shield could make it much more useful, especially because shields fall off so hard later in the game. Difficulty: I think that DM is harder than StS. Maybe it's just that StS has better deck themes to exploit, but in DM, I was using all of the optional boons from the start and was only able to finish a single complete run within 7 hours. For all intents and purposes, if I enable every possible buff that lowers my end score, the game should be considered easy mode, but that isn’t so much the case here. Speaking of buffs, I do really like how the difficulty works. You choose different modifiers that help or hinder your gameplay to create a type of personalized difficulty. [h1] [b] Graphics (Quality/Performance) – [7/10] [/b] [/h1] Quality: The one area that DM surpasses StS in my opinion is the graphics and animations. There are battle animations and movements here in DM that StS simply doesn’t have without mods. Aside from that, the UI is also almost the same, which is a great thing because StS has a wonderful UI that shows the player tons of information, so if anything were to be copied it should definitely be the UI. You can mouse over icons to see what they do and cards define their abilities when hovered over. Even easier here in DM is to quickly view the card upgrade by right-clicking. Great job. Performance: I encountered no bugs or performance issues. i9-13900KF | RTX 4090 | 64GB RAM | 1440p @ 240hz | installed on SSD [h1] [b] Audio (Sound Effects/Music) – [3/10] [/b] [/h1] Sound Effects: Basic. Cards and match board all have sound effects. There is no voice acting that I noticed. Music: Nothing really interesting. [h1] [b] Replay Factor (Longevity) – [5/10] [/b] [/h1] Not tons of replay value, but decent, as expected with most roguelikes. You can do repeat runs to unlock cards and trinkets. Aside from unlocks and achievements, there are no leaderboards or daily runs. DM could really use some sort of online aspect to have longevity. [h1] [b] Final Verdict – [6/10] [/b] [/h1] Demon’s Mirror brings some good and unique concepts to the CCG roguelike area. TL;DR This is an enjoyable enough deckbuilder with a twist of chaining items on a board for resources, but with a direct competitor like Across the Obelisk out there, the slower pace of runs, the less innovative map design, lack of character progression, and anemic storylines, you will get the most enjoyment if you prefer the revealed mechanics of new cards and items that happen after multiple runs in the game. Longer version: This is a deckbuilder that clearly has been built on the legacy of games like Slay the Spire, but whose immediate visual and mechanical precursor is the very deep and expansive Across the Obelisk. You have a number of action points per round that can be spent on playing cards (the games main twist) to collect resources from a board in a "link in a chain all the same type of resource." As many people have stated before in reviews, this is not the same as match-3 mechanics, so while the grid may make you think it will play like the match-3 combat mechanics of older games like Puzzlequest, this is a different beast altogether. The match board's resources are your primary way of getting large resources; while attack cards in your hand might do some damage, a long chain of crossed swords will usually do more. A shield card in your hand might only give you 3 or 4 damage mitigation for that round, whereas a long chain of shields might give you 7-14. The two other resources (green energy and diamonds) work to enhance or fire off effects. the problem is that when you generally start with 3 action points a round and collecting one chain of resource son the board usually costs 2 (though there are various mechanics of mitigation of that cost) the game feels like it is creating an exhausting opportunity cost to try and look to chaining resources (the game's more unique mechanic). This is particularly true of the green energy resource, whose presence can enhance some cards (if you have x amount of green banked, some cards might add near double their normal effect value, for example) or be spent as a required resource costs for some cards that require both green and an action point cost. Why is that a problem? The green resource decays by half every turn, making it feel a bit punishing to collect. There are three different characters you can play that each have their own card pools: A bruiser with basic mechanics; an enchanter whose unique twist is the "influence" mechanic, that permanently reduces health bars, cannot be removed or healed by monsters, and bypasses shields; and an archer whose "shock" mechanic is a damaging debuff that starts at a counter number (say 3) and then every time you gather resources from the board, it fires off once damaging the creature for the amount of chock they have and reduces the shock counter on them by one. Each hero has a different mechanic in their cards to manipulate the board in some manner with cards that usually cost no action points. The mechanics shine best in some of the combat designs, particularly a few bosses. One standout boss is a two faced creature that alternately shields it's front or back -- when you chain damage from the resource board it hits the "back", when you do damage from a card it hits the "front." As soon as you hit the creature it swaps it's shield orientation, making the order of operations in your attacks more thoughtful. However, the game suffers in a number of ways compared to it's Across the Obelisk competitor. 1. The storyline is barely extant and unlocking the conditions to defeat the "hidden final boss" ends up feeling a bit anticlimatic after you do it. The very cool monster designs just don't really hint at any greater worldbuilding and while visually cohesive, it really feels generic. 2. the "branching map nodes" that are common in games like this (Slay the Spire (StS), Across the Obelisk(AtO)) are here as well, but implemented in a manner that feels pretty basic and not very interesting. Unlike AtO, interetsing questline events are completely random, so when you get a random event, ti doesn't usually drive you to seek out specific other pathways to complete the quest. (There is a small exception with an event like the dragon egg, but mostly they are just random and don't lead to significant changes in your path choices.) Most routes have only a few branching choices and some of the paths are a bit nonsensical (for example, you might enter a shop tile and buy stuff with your gold. The next node is a random event with no branching pathway, The next is another shop -- and since most random events don't gain you gold, it's kind of silly not to at least put a choice of a combat encounter spaced between them.) 3. Deckbuilders have three important basic mechanics at their heart: acquiring new cards, upgrading cards in your hand, and pruning cards from your deck. Demon's mirror after multiple runs does have some interesting card variety for each hero, allowing them to be built a few different ways, and each combat gives you a choice of three possible cards to acquire. Upgrading a card is uncommon but feels fair enough, but PRUNING cards is super rare and is paced pretty poorly. 4. While there is a set of buffs and debuffs you can choose as you make successful runs in the game to increase challenge (think the mirror in Hades, and again you see this is AtO) there is zero character progression (more StS than AtO or Hades) so that completing runs does not give you nee options to buffs, starting cards, or other unlocks that might increase the game's longevity. Again, it is a good game and I have put over 60 hours into it, so I have enjoyed it. I just wish the devs would tweak it a bit more. Imagine if after each run you got a temporary boon for the next run without increasing the difficulty, and each run whenever you successfully finished all three worlds gave a minor permanent buff / skill and finishing off the final boss gave a great permanent buff. This could be anything from thinsg liek giving a chance to purge a card after every x number of combats or after every miniboss and boss (increasing risk/ reward mechanics.) Maybe you might get a buff that makes the first card upgrade at shops free. maybe you could have revealed the name of some of the random events on the map which might help you more strategically plan out your route. Maybe you could start with a specific card in your deck, certain cards being upgraded, reduce the decay of green sources each round, diminish the number of diamonds you need to collect before firing off your special power -- there are lots of interesting possibilities here that would play to the mechanics-focused game here, because there just isn't any story reward worth mentioning. This is a polished, enjoyable game that only suffers from some stiff direct competition with AtO. The mechanics make for longer runs so it also doesn't quite feel as snappy as some competitor roguelike / roguelite deckbuilders, the story is thin and there could really be more / better incentives for repeated runs. But it is slick, polished, focused on mechanics first and worth your time if you are willing to get past the initial very constraining opening few runs. Oh, and ♥♥♥♥ the smoke monster miniboss that punishes you for using skill cards (which make up about half of your cards, including all cards that manipulate thr board and cards that shield you). That fight is worse than most of the bosses and really could use rebalancing.
